title: Circles
short: Tangents to a circle and the number of tangents from a point.
lede: Two theorems and a handful of standard figures cover this chapter.
lens: The rest of the **15-mark Geometry unit**, roughly **5–6 marks**.
Expect a tangent-length proof (3 marks) and objective questions on the number of tangents from a point.
concepts: **1. Tangent.** A line that touches the circle at exactly one point. That point is the **point of contact**.
**2. Theorem 10.1.** The tangent at any point of a circle is **perpendicular** to the radius through the point of contact.
**3. Theorem 10.2.** The lengths of tangents drawn from an **external point** to a circle are **equal**.

**4. Standard consequences.** A tangent is parallel to the tangent at the opposite end of a diameter; a parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus; and the angle between two tangents from an external point is supplementary to the angle subtended by the chord of contact at the centre.
formulas: Tangent ⊥ radius at the point of contact
PA = PB for tangents from an external point P
Tangent length = √(d² − r²), where d is the distance from the centre
tricks: - **Always join the centre to the point of contact.** That creates the right angle you need, and it is the first line of almost every proof here.
- For a triangle circumscribing a circle, let the tangent segments from each vertex be x, y, z. The three side lengths give three equations, and the perimeter is 2(x + y + z).
- “Prove the tangents are equal” is done by joining the centre to both points of contact and to the external point, then using RHS congruence.
- The angle between two tangents and the angle at the centre **add to 180°**.
mistakes: - Forgetting to state that the radius is perpendicular to the tangent — that is a marked step.
- Assuming the two tangent lengths are equal when the point is inside or on the circle.
- In the circumscribed-triangle problem, mixing up which segment belongs to which vertex.
- Writing “the angle is 90°” without naming the theorem that gives it.

qa.q: How many tangents can be drawn from a point inside a circle?
qa.a: None. A line through an interior point must cut the circle at two points.

qa.q: From a point 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm, a tangent is drawn. Find its length.
a: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so the three lengths form a right triangle.

qa.q: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. If ∠POQ = 110°, find ∠PTQ.
qa.a: The radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact, so ∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90°. In quadrilateral POQT: ∠PTQ = 360° − (90° + 90° + 110°) = 70°.

qa.q: Prove that the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
a: Let P be the external point and PA, PB the tangents with points of contact A and B.
Join OA, OB and OP.
In ΔOAP and ΔOBP: OA = OB (radii), OP is common, and ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90° (tangent ⊥ radius).
By RHS congruence, ΔOAP ≅ ΔOBP, so PA = PB.

qa.q: A student says, “From every point P in the plane, exactly two equal tangents can be drawn to a given circle.” Test the claim for a point outside the circle, on the circle and inside the circle.
a: P **outside** the circle: exactly two tangents can be drawn, and their lengths are equal.
P **on** the circle: exactly one tangent can be drawn (at P itself); there is no pair of tangents.
P **inside** the circle: no tangent exists, since every line through P cuts the circle in two points. So the claim holds only for an external point.

qa.q: The tangent at a point P of a circle of radius 5 cm meets a line through the centre O at Q, where OQ = 12 cm. Find the length PQ.
a: The tangent at P is perpendicular to the radius OP, so ∠OPQ = 90°.
In the right triangle OPQ: PQ² = OQ² − OP² = 144 − 25 = 119.

qa.q: Prove that a chord of the larger of two concentric circles which touches the smaller circle is bisected at the point of contact.
a: Let the chord AB of the larger circle touch the smaller circle at P; O is the common centre.
OP is a radius of the smaller circle and AB is a tangent to it, so OP ⊥ AB.
In the larger circle, the perpendicular drawn from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
Hence AP = PB: the chord is bisected at the point of contact.

qa.q: Prove that the angle between two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle is supplementary to the angle subtended by the line joining the points of contact at the centre.
a: Let TP and TQ be tangents from T, touching the circle at P and Q.
∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90° because a radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact.
In quadrilateral POQT the angles sum to 360°, so ∠PTQ + ∠POQ = 360° − 180° = 180°.
Therefore the two angles are supplementary.

qa.q: A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle. Prove that AB + CD = AD + BC.
a: Let the tangent segments from A, B, C, D be p, q, r, s respectively.
Then AB = p + q, BC = q + r, CD = r + s and AD = p + s.
AB + CD = p + q + r + s and AD + BC = p + s + q + r.
The two sums are identical, so AB + CD = AD + BC.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

From an external point T, two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O. It is given that ∠PTQ = 70°.

(a) State why ∠OPT = 90°.
(b) Find ∠POQ.
(c) Find ∠OPQ.
a: (a) The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
(b) In quadrilateral OPTQ, ∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90°, so ∠POQ = 360° − 90° − 90° − 70° = **110°**.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A circle is inscribed in ΔABC and touches the sides BC, CA and AB at D, E and F respectively. AB = 12 cm, BC = 8 cm and CA = 10 cm.

(a) Which tangent lengths are equal?
(b) Find AF, BD and CE.
(c) Verify your answers against the three given sides.
a: (a) Tangents from one point are equal: AF = AE, BF = BD and CD = CE.
(b) Let AF = x, BD = y, CE = z. Then x + y = 12, y + z = 8, z + x = 10, so x + y + z = 15. Hence **AF = 7 cm, BD = 5 cm, CE = 3 cm**.

qa.q: Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
a: Given: a circle with centre O and a tangent XY touching it at P. To prove: OP ⊥ XY.
Take any other point Q on XY and join OQ.
The tangent meets the circle only at P, so Q lies outside the circle. Hence OQ is longer than the radius: OQ > OP.
This is true for every point Q other than P on XY, so OP is the shortest distance from O to the line XY.
The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular, so OP ⊥ XY. ∎

mcq.q: The number of tangents from a point on the circle is: (a) 0  (b) 1  (c) 2  (d) infinite
The angle between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact is: (a) 45°  (b) 60°  (c) 90°  (d) 180°
Two tangents from an external point to a circle are: (a) unequal  (b) always perpendicular  (c) parallel  (d) equal
mcq.a: **(d) Equal.**

mcq.q: A tangent to a circle meets the circle in: (a) exactly one point  (b) no point  (c) exactly two points  (d) infinitely many points
mcq.a: **(a) exactly one point.** By definition, a tangent touches the circle at exactly one point, the point of contact.

mcq.q: If the angle between two tangents drawn from an external point P to a circle of radius a and centre O is 60°, then OP = (a) a√3  (b) a√2  (c) a/2  (d) 2a
mcq.a: **(d) 2a.** ∠APB = 60° gives ∠APO = 30° and, in right triangle OAP, OA = OP sin 30°, so OP = a/(1/2) = 2a.

mcq.q: The number of tangents that can be drawn from a point outside a circle is: (a) 1  (b) 2  (c) 3  (d) infinite
mcq.a: **(b) 2.** Exactly two, and they are equal in length.

mcq.q: A line that cuts a circle in two distinct points is called a: (a) secant  (b) tangent  (c) chord  (d) diameter
mcq.a: **(a) secant.** A tangent meets the circle at one point; a chord is the segment joining the two points.

mcq.q: A tangent of length 24 cm is drawn from a point 25 cm from the centre. The radius is: (a) 24 cm  (b) 12 cm  (c) 7 cm  (d) 5 cm

trend: One tangent-length proof or numerical (3 marks) and objective questions on the number of tangents.
onepager: - Tangent ⊥ radius at the point of contact.
- Tangents from one external point are equal.
task: Draw a circle, take an external point, and construct both tangents with compass and ruler. Measure them — they should match, which is Theorem 10.2 in your hand.
steps: 1. Note whether the line **touches** (tangent, one point), **cuts** (secant, two points) or **misses** the circle — the number of intersections decides the whole theorem.
2. Recall the two core facts: the **tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact**, and **tangents from an external point are equal in length**.
3. When two tangents are drawn from an external point, join the centre to that point: it **bisects the angle between the tangents** and the line joining the points of contact is bisected by it.
4. In the proof, name the theorem you used at each step and finish with the **angle or length** asked for, with units where relevant.

title: Areas Related to Circles
lede: Perimeter of a sector and area of a segment — two formulas and a lot of care with the radius.
lens: Part of the **10-mark Mensuration unit**, roughly **4–5 marks**.
Typically one question on the perimeter or area of a sector, and one on a segment or a combined figure.
Only sectors and segments of a circle remain in the rationalised syllabus.
concepts: **1. Sector.** The region between two radii and the arc joining their endpoints. The angle at the centre is θ.
**2. Segment.** The region between a chord and the arc it cuts off. The minor segment uses the minor arc.

head: Quantity
Formula (θ in degrees)
rows: Area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord
Area of sector − area of that triangle

concepts: **3. Combined figures.** Most questions are a square or rectangle with quadrant-shaped corners removed, or a circle inscribed in a square. Subtract the parts you do not want.
**4. Circle inscribed in a square:** the diameter equals the side. **Circle circumscribing a square:** the diameter equals the diagonal, `a√2`.
formulas: Segment area = sector area − ½ r² sin θ
Perimeter of a sector = 2r + arc length
tricks: - **Perimeter of a sector is 2r + arc**, not just the arc. Missing the two radii is the most common error here.
- For θ = 90° the sector area is exactly one quarter of πr²; for θ = 60°, one sixth.
- Circle inscribed in a square of side a: wasted area = a² − πa²/4. Circle circumscribing it: wasted area = πa²/2 − a².
- Take π as 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7 — the arithmetic collapses. Otherwise use 3.14.
mistakes: - Forgetting to add the two radii to the perimeter of a sector.
- Using the diameter where the formula needs the radius.
- Computing the segment as sector minus chord *length* instead of sector minus **triangle area**.
- Mixing degrees and radians. The CBSE formulas use degrees only.

qa.q: Find the length of an arc of a sector with radius 21 cm and central angle 120°.
qa.a: Arc length = (θ/360°) × 2πr = (120/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 21 = (1/3) × 132 = **44 cm**. Use 22/7 for π whenever the radius is a multiple of 7, as it is here — the sevens cancel and the arithmetic stays exact.

qa.q: The circumference of a circle exceeds its diameter by 30 cm. Find the radius (take π = 22/7).
qa.a: 2πr − 2r = 30 ⇒ 2r(22/7 − 1) = 30 ⇒ 2r(15/7) = 30 ⇒ r = 7 cm. Check: circumference 44 cm, diameter 14 cm, difference 30 cm.

qa.q: Find the area of a sector of radius 6 cm with a central angle of 60° (take π = 3.14).
qa.a: Area of sector = (θ/360°) × πr² = (60/360) × 3.14 × 36 = (1/6) × 113.04 = **18.84 cm²**. Here the radius is not a multiple of 7, so π = 3.14 as the question directs, and the unit is cm² because this is an area, not a length.

qa.q: Find the perimeter of a sector with radius 14 cm and central angle 90°.
a: Perimeter = 2(14) + 22 = 50 cm.

qa.q: A student finds the area of a circular pond of diameter 28 m as (22/7) × 28² = 2464 m². Identify the error and give the correct area.
a: Error: the formula πr² needs the **radius**, but the student substituted the diameter 28 m.
Radius = 28 ÷ 2 = 14 m.
Area = (22/7) × 14² = (22/7) × 196 = **616 m²** (one-fourth of the wrong value).

qa.q: A horse is tied to a peg at one corner of a square field of side 15 m by a rope 5 m long. Find the area of the field over which the horse can graze. (Take π = 3.14.)
a: The horse can reach points within 5 m of the corner, but only inside the field, which spans a 90° angle at that corner.
So the grazing region is a quadrant (sector of 90°) of radius 5 m.

qa.q: Find the area of the minor segment of a circle of radius 14 cm whose central angle is 90° (π = 22/7).
a: Area of the right triangle formed by the two radii = ½ × 14 × 14 = 98 cm².
Area of the minor segment = 154 − 98 = 56 cm².

qa.q: A square of side 14 cm has a circle inscribed in it. Find the area between the square and the circle.
a: The inscribed circle has diameter 14 cm, so radius 7 cm.
Area of square = 196 cm². Area of circle = (22/7) × 49 = 154 cm².
Required area = 196 − 154 = 42 cm².

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A pizza of radius 14 cm is cut into 8 equal slices. (Take π = 22/7.)

(a) What is the central angle of each slice?
(b) What is the area of one slice?
(c) What is the perimeter of one slice, counting both straight edges?

Read and answer:

A circular park of radius 14 m is surrounded by a path 7 m wide. (Take π = 22/7.)

(a) What is the outer radius of the path?
(b) What is the area of the path?
(c) What is the cost of paving it at Rs 40 per m²?
a: (a) Outer radius = 14 + 7 = **21 m**.

qa.q: Two circles touch externally. The sum of their areas is 130π cm² and the distance between their centres is 14 cm. Find their radii.
a: Let the radii be r₁ and r₂. Since they touch externally, r₁ + r₂ = 14.
πr₁² + πr₂² = 130π ⇒ r₁² + r₂² = 130.
(r₁ + r₂)² = r₁² + r₂² + 2r₁r₂ ⇒ 196 = 130 + 2r₁r₂ ⇒ r₁r₂ = 33.
So r₁ and r₂ are roots of t² − 14t + 33 = 0, giving 11 cm and 3 cm.

qa.q: The minute hand of a clock is 14 cm long. Find (i) the angle it turns in 10 minutes, (ii) the distance moved by its tip in that time and (iii) the area swept by the hand. (Take π = 22/7.)
a: (i) The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, so in 10 minutes it turns 60°.
(ii) The tip moves along an arc of a circle of radius 14 cm: arc = (60/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 14 = ⅙ × 88 = 44/3 cm ≈ **14.67 cm**.
(iii) The hand sweeps a sector of angle 60°: area = (60/360) × (22/7) × 14² = ⅙ × 616 = 308/3 cm² ≈ **102.67 cm²**.

mcq.q: The area of a quadrant of a circle of radius r is: (a) πr²/2  (b) 2πr  (c) πr²  (d) πr²/4
The perimeter of a sector includes: (a) only the arc  (b) the arc and one radius  (c) the arc and two radii  (d) the chord and the arc
mcq.a: **(c) The arc and two radii.**

mcq.q: The area of a segment is found by: (a) sector − triangle  (b) sector + triangle  (c) circle − sector  (d) triangle − sector
mcq.a: **(a) Sector − triangle.**

mcq.q: The length of the arc of a sector of angle θ in a circle of radius r is: (a) (θ/360°) × πr²  (b) (θ/180°) × πr²  (c) (θ/360°) × 2r  (d) (θ/360°) × 2πr
mcq.a: **(d) (θ/360°) × 2πr.** The arc is the fraction θ/360° of the whole circumference 2πr.

mcq.q: The area of a sector of a circle of radius 7 cm with central angle 90° is (π = 22/7): (a) 77 cm²  (b) 38.5 cm²  (c) 154 cm²  (d) 19.25 cm²
The area of a circle whose circumference is 44 cm is: (a) 616 cm²  (b) 308 cm²  (c) 154 cm²  (d) 77 cm²
mcq.a: **(c) 154 cm².** 2πr = 44 gives r = 7 cm, so the area is πr² = 154 cm².

mcq.q: If the radius of a circle is doubled, its area becomes: (a) 2 times  (b) 4 times  (c) 8 times  (d) unchanged
mcq.a: **(b) 4 times.** Area ∝ r², so doubling r multiplies the area by 2² = 4.

mcq.q: The area of a semicircle of radius r is: (a) πr²/2  (b) πr²  (c) 2πr  (d) πr²/4
mcq.a: **(a) πr²/2.** A semicircle is half of a full circle.

trend: One sector perimeter/area question and one combined-figure question. Quadrant corners cut from a square is the classic combined figure.
onepager: - Inscribed circle: diameter = side of square.
task: Cut four identical quadrants from the corners of a square card and lay them together — they form exactly one full circle when the radius is half the side.
steps: 1. List the **radius or diameter** first, then decide what the question is asking for — circumference, area of a circle, length of an arc, area of a sector, or area of a segment.
2. Use the angle at the centre: **arc length = (θ/360°) × 2πr** and **area of sector = (θ/360°) × πr²**.
3. For a **segment**, subtract the triangle from the sector: minor segment = sector − triangle, and for θ = 60°, 90° or 120° the triangle part is usually found by ½r² sin θ or by the standard values.
4. For combined figures, **add or subtract whole shapes** and never add a part twice. Keep π as 22/7 only when the radius is a multiple of 7, otherwise use 3.14, and state the unit as cm or cm².

title: Surface Areas and Volumes
short: Combinations of solids, conversion of solids, and the frustum.
lede: A table of formulas plus three standard question types. The frustum is worth learning separately.
lens: The rest of the **10-mark Mensuration unit**, roughly **5–6 marks**.
Expect one question on a combination of solids (3–4 marks) and one on conversion of solids or a frustum (3–4 marks).
Surface area questions almost always involve **removing** a surface where two solids join — that is where the marks are.
concepts: **1. Combinations of solids.** A solid made of two or more basic solids. Total surface area = sum of the *curved/lateral* surface areas actually exposed. Where two solids join, the joining face is **not** part of the outer surface.
**2. Volume is additive.** Unlike surface area, the volume of a combination is simply the sum of the volumes of its parts.
**3. Conversion of solids.** When one solid is melted and recast into another, or many small solids are combined into one, **the volume stays the same**. Set volume before = volume after and solve.
**4. Frustum of a cone.** The part of a cone left after a smaller cone is cut off the top by a plane parallel to the base. Its slant height is `l = √[h² + (R − r)²]`.

**5. Cylindrical hole drilled through a solid.** Subtract the cylinder’s volume, but its curved surface is now **exposed**, so add it to the surface area. Then remove the two circular faces where it was drilled.
formulas: Cone: CSA = πrl,  V = πr²h/3,  l = √(r² + h²)
Frustum: l = √[h² + (R − r)²],  CSA = π(R + r)l
Total surface area of a frustum = π(R + r)l + πR² + πr²
steps: 1. Sketch the solid and label every dimension, including any that must be inferred (for example the height of a cone placed on a cylinder).
2. Decide what is **exposed**. Cross out joining faces on the sketch.
3. Write the formula for each part separately before substituting anything.
4. For conversion problems, write *volume before = volume after* first, then substitute.
5. Give the final answer with units, and to the number of decimal places asked (usually two, with π = 22/7 or 3.14 as specified).
tricks: - **Hemisphere on top of a cuboid or cylinder:** the flat circular base of the hemisphere is *not* part of the outer surface. Use only its curved area, 2πr².
- **Cone on top of a cylinder with the same radius:** the joining circular face disappears from the surface area, but both heights add in the volume.
- **Conversion problems are one equation.** Number of small spheres × volume of one = volume of the big one. Do not compute individual volumes first.
- **Frustum slant height uses (R − r), not (R + r).** That single sign decides the whole answer.
- When a question says “slant height” is given, do not recompute it from r and h.
mistakes: - Including the joining face in the total surface area.
- Using πr²h for a cone instead of πr²h/3.
- Forgetting to divide by 3 for cones and pyramids.
- In conversion problems, equating *surface areas* instead of volumes. Melting preserves volume, never surface area.
- Writing the answer without units, or with the wrong unit (cm² for area, cm³ for volume).

qa.q: Find the total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm (π = 22/7).
qa.a: Total surface area of a solid hemisphere = 3πr² = 3 × (22/7) × 49 = 462 cm² (curved 308 + flat circular face 154).

qa.q: A solid consists of a cylinder with a hemisphere on one end and a cone on the other, all of radius 7 cm. The cylinder is 20 cm high, the cone 12 cm high. Find the total surface area (take π = 22/7).
a: Cylinder CSA = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 20 = 880 cm².
Hemisphere CSA = 2 × (22/7) × 49 = 308 cm².
Cone slant height l = √(7² + 12²) = √193 ≈ 13.89 cm, so cone CSA = (22/7) × 7 × 13.89 ≈ 305.6 cm².
Total ≈ 880 + 308 + 305.6 = 1493.6 cm². The two circular joining faces are not counted.

qa.q: A solid metallic sphere of radius 4.2 cm is melted and recast into a cylinder of radius 6 cm. Find the height of the cylinder.
a: Volume of sphere = volume of cylinder.

qa.q: A student finds the volume of a cone with r = 7 cm and h = 12 cm as (22/7) × 7² × 12 = 1848 cm³. Identify the error and give the correct volume.
a: Error: that is the volume of the **cylinder** of the same base and height. A cone holds one-third of it.
Correct formula: V = ⅓πr²h.

qa.q: A toy is a cone mounted on a hemisphere of the same base radius 3.5 cm. The total height of the toy is 15.5 cm. Find its total surface area. (Take π = 22/7.)
a: Height of the cone = 15.5 − 3.5 = 12 cm, so slant height l = √(3.5² + 12²) = √156.25 = 12.5 cm.
Curved surface of the cone = πrl = (22/7) × 3.5 × 12.5 = 137.5 cm²; curved surface of the hemisphere = 2πr² = 77 cm².
Total surface area = 137.5 + 77 = **214.5 cm²**. (The joining circle is inside, so it is not counted.)

qa.q: A cylindrical bucket 32 cm high with base radius 18 cm is emptied to form a conical heap of sand 24 cm high. Find the radius of the heap.
a: Volumes are equal: π(18)²(32) = (1/3)πr²(24).
So r = 36 cm. (The height of the heap is ¼ of the cylinder’s, but the radius works out larger.)

qa.q: A cylindrical vessel of radius 6 cm and height 12 cm is full of water. How many conical cups of radius 2 cm and height 6 cm can be filled from it?
a: Volume of the vessel = π × 6² × 12 = 432π cm³.
Volume of one cup = (1/3)π × 2² × 6 = 8π cm³.
Number of cups = 432π ÷ 8π = 54.
So 54 conical cups can be filled.

qa.q: 100 solid iron spheres, each of radius 1 cm, are melted to form one solid sphere. Find its radius.
a: Total volume is conserved: 100 × (4/3)π(1)³ = (4/3)πR³.
Cancelling (4/3)π: R³ = 100, so R = ∛100 ≈ 4.64 cm.

qa.q: A frustum of a cone has radii 14 cm and 7 cm and height 24 cm. Find its slant height and curved surface area (take π = 22/7).

Read and answer:

A cylindrical water tank has a diameter of 4 m and a height of 7 m. (Take π = 22/7.)

(a) Find its volume in m³.
(b) How many litres can it hold? (1 m³ = 1000 litres)
(c) A family uses 400 litres a day. For how many days will a full tank last?

Read and answer:

A metal cuboid of dimensions 44 cm × 21 cm × 12 cm is melted and recast into a solid cylinder of radius 7 cm. (Take π = 22/7.)

(a) Find the volume of the cuboid.
(b) Find the height of the cylinder.
(c) Why is the volume, and not the surface area, equated?
a: (c) Melting and recasting changes the shape but not the amount of metal, so the volume is conserved; the surface area changes.

qa.q: A drinking glass is shaped like a frustum of a cone with height 14 cm and end diameters 4 cm and 2 cm. Find its capacity.
a: R = 2 cm, r = 1 cm, h = 14 cm.

mcq.q: The volume of a cone of radius r and height h is: (a) πr²h  (b) πr²h/3  (c) 2πr²h  (d) πrh
When a solid is melted and recast into another shape, which quantity is conserved? (a) surface area  (b) volume  (c) both  (d) neither
mcq.a: **(b) Volume.** Surface area almost always changes.

mcq.q: The slant height of a frustum with radii R and r and height h is: (a) √[h² + (R − r)²]  (b) √[h² + (R + r)²]  (c) h + R + r  (d) √(R² − r²)
The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius r is: (a) 2πr²  (b) 4πr²  (c) 3πr²  (d) πr²
mcq.a: **(c) 3πr².** Curved surface 2πr² plus the flat circular face πr² gives 3πr².

mcq.q: If the radius of a sphere is doubled, its volume becomes: (a) 2 times  (b) 4 times  (c) 6 times  (d) 8 times
mcq.a: **(d) 8 times.** V = (4/3)πr³, so doubling r multiplies the volume by 2³ = 8.

mcq.q: The curved surface area of a cylinder of radius r and height h is: (a) πr²h  (b) 2πr(r + h)  (c) 2πrh  (d) πrl
mcq.a: **(c) 2πrh.** 2πr(r + h) is the total surface area and πr²h is the volume.

mcq.q: The volume of a sphere of radius r is: (a) (4/3)πr³  (b) 4πr²  (c) (2/3)πr³  (d) πr³
mcq.a: **(a) (4/3)πr³.** 4πr² is the surface area of the sphere.

mcq.q: A cone, a hemisphere and a cylinder have equal bases and equal heights. The ratio of their volumes is: (a) 2 : 3 : 1  (b) 3 : 1 : 2  (c) 1 : 3 : 2  (d) 1 : 2 : 3
mcq.a: **(d) 1 : 2 : 3.** With radius = height = r: πr³/3 : 2πr³/3 : πr³.

trend: One combination-of-solids surface area question and one conversion or frustum question appear most years. The frustum has been asked repeatedly since it was retained in the syllabus.
onepager: - Surface area: count only what is exposed. Volume: always additive.
- Melting conserves volume, never surface area.
- Cone volume has the 1/3. Hemisphere CSA is 2πr², TSA is 3πr².
task: Take a cylindrical container and a cone of the same radius and height. Fill the cone with water and pour it into the cylinder three times — it should exactly fill it. That is the 1/3 in the cone formula.
